assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data opened up the measurement of intergenerational mobility and of place-based causal effects on children's outcomes. This changed how economists, and policymakers, study opportunity. It combines new data with a framework for identifying causal neighbourhood effects, which fits the view that data discovery plus an explanatory framework together make a scientific contribution. The influence on the field and on policy debate is large.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear intellectual leader of the programme and Hendren is the central co-author on causal place effects. Friedman and Katz are important collaborators (Katz's work on Moving to Opportunity), but a three-person cap forces a judgement. Credit is concentrated enough to support a prize without being obviously arbitrary.
assessment.maturity: The core papers date from about 2014 to 2022 and have been replicated or extended with multiple datasets and countries. Influence is already substantial, though the timescale is shorter than for some other candidates.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as a measurement and data contribution or as a conceptual one
How the credit should be split among Chetty, Hendren and Friedman
Some debate over the interpretation of place effects and the robustness of mobility estimates
Overlap with Katz's role in B009, which may affect how credit is allocated across the list

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Work on how technology and trade reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality has changed both research and public discussion. The China-shock design is a leading example of credible, quasi-experimental evidence on large-scale adjustment costs. The task-based approach and the education-versus-technology framework explain wage structure. The contribution is broad and has had a lasting impact on society.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both the task framework and the trade-shock papers. Hanson is central to the trade-adjustment evidence. Katz is central to the long-run skill-premium literature. Dorn is a key co-author on the China shock but is left out by the cap. The task approach also builds on work by Levy and Murnane that is not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Foundational papers span the late 1990s to the 2010s, with extensive replication and follow-up, so the evidence base is mature. Priority is spread across several strands.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2023 prize (Goldin) and the 2024 prize (Acemoglu, technology and institutions) may affect the committee's appetite
Several strands (skill-biased change, tasks, trade shocks) may be seen as separate contributions
Dorn's exclusion and the missing Levy and Murnane credit complicate attribution
Debate over the external validity of the China-shock estimates

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Heterogeneous-firm trade models shifted the field's unit of analysis from industries to firms. They explain selection, reallocation and a new channel for gains from trade, and they changed both theory and empirical practice. The ideas diffused widely into macroeconomics, development and industrial organisation.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the pivotal contribution. Helpman has a major role through the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work and his broader theory programme. Redding has important quantitative extensions but is more recent. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum also have strong priority claims that this ballot item does not credit.
assessment.maturity: The central models date from 2003 and are thoroughly tested and incorporated into textbooks. The evidence is mature.
uncertainties: Priority questions concerning Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not in the credited names
Krugman's 2008 prize partly overlaps in subject
Helpman may be seen as the stronger candidate through B049, creating allocation tension

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Weak-instrument diagnostics and identification-robust inference changed everyday applied practice. They improved the credibility of instrumental-variables work in labour, public and development economics, which makes them a methodological contribution with broad empirical reach. The Staiger-Stock results on the weak-instrument problem are among the most widely used in applied microeconomics.
assessment.attribution: Staiger and Stock define the problem and give the practical diagnostics. Andrews contributes the general theory of robust inference. Moreira and Yogo are important but more specialised contributors. Credit within the econometrics community is fairly clear, though the field has several overlapping strands.
assessment.maturity: Foundational results date from the 1990s and 2000s, and practice has changed accordingly, so the evidence of impact is mature.
uncertainties: The committee may prefer applied or conceptual breakthroughs to technical econometric refinements
Stock and Andrews also appear in other econometrics ballot items, so credit may be split
Possible tension between the identification and the testing contributions

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Field-experimental and audit-style evidence on labour-market discrimination converted a contested issue into credible causal measurement. The work shaped research on discrimination, hiring and bias and has had a large effect on policy and public debate. It rests on a design that is simple, transparent and extensible.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 Bertrand-Mullainathan résumé study is the signature contribution. The wider audit and correspondence literature has many contributors, including Charles, Pager and others, and the longlist credits only part of it. A prize centred on this one study may therefore overstate their claim to the whole field.
assessment.maturity: The central paper is more than twenty years old, with extensive replication. The method and findings are well established.
uncertainties: The breadth of the audit-study literature makes the credited set contestable
Questions about whether the method measures discrimination or differential signals
The 2023 prize on gender in labour markets may reduce the committee's appetite for adjacent topics

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Machine-learning methods for causal inference (double or debiased ML, causal forests, heterogeneous effects) are changing empirical practice and connecting economics with data science. The methodological reach is broad and still growing, with many applications in policy evaluation.
assessment.attribution: Chernozhukov, with co-authors, developed the debiased ML framework. Athey and Wager developed the causal forest approach and Athey was a major influence on the field. Many co-authors contributed, and the broader literature includes related work by others, so attribution is diffuse.
assessment.maturity: Key papers date from about 2016 to 2018, so the field is quite young. Long-run influence is promising but not yet fully tested.
uncertainties: Imbens's 2021 prize on causal inference may reduce the appetite for adjacent methods
Maturity: it is not yet clear which ideas will prove durable
Attribution among Athey, Wager, Chernozhukov and their many co-authors
Athey also appears in B029, which may complicate credit

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Research on agglomeration, cities and the sources of urban productivity gives microfoundations for why economic activity clusters. It includes empirical evidence on sorting, human capital externalities and housing. It matters for policy on land use, housing and regional inequality.
assessment.attribution: Duranton and Puga provide the microfoundations for agglomeration. Glaeser provides broad empirical and conceptual contributions on cities and human capital. Moretti and Gyourko are important contributors on local labour markets and housing. The field is wide, so the credited set could appear arbitrary, and Krugman's earlier prize already covers part of the underlying theory.
assessment.maturity: Core contributions span the 1990s to the 2010s and have been widely used. The empirical consensus is reasonably mature though some sub-areas are still developing.
uncertainties: Overlap with Krugman's 2008 prize on economic geography
Breadth of the field versus concentration of credit
Identification challenges in estimating agglomeration externalities

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bayesian persuasion offers a tractable framework for how a sender's information-disclosure choices shape decisions. It has spread into theory, industrial organisation, political economy and applications such as media, regulation and market design. The conceptual contribution is clear and general.
assessment.attribution: Kamenica and Gentzkow's 2011 paper defines the model. Bergemann and Morris generalised and unified it as information design, so credit is plausibly shared. A three-person cap would force a choice among four strong contributors.
assessment.maturity: The framework dates from 2011, with growing but still limited empirical validation. Theoretical influence is high, though applied testing is thinner than for many other candidates.
uncertainties: Maturity of empirical and policy impact
How to divide credit between Kamenica-Gentzkow and Bergemann-Morris
Gentzkow's separate empirical contributions might complicate how his credit is framed
